## tl;dr We read the HTTP response headers of 217,097,223 page responses from Common Crawl, 10% of its September 2026 crawl of 2.17 billion pages, and looked for any header written for an AI system. 7,959 sites sent one. Almost all of them point agents to another resource, such as an llms.txt file or an MCP server. A small number try to give the agent orders. Whether any of it reaches your model depends on which parts of the response your fetch tool passes along, so the defense starts there. - 7,959 sites sent a header aimed at AI. Writing to agents through headers is already routine, so treat headers as part of what your agents read. - 7,271 of those sites sent pointers, and 6,989 of them sent x-llms-txt . A pointer is the server telling your agent where to go next. Check that your agents treat those destinations as new, untrusted fetches. - 30 sites sent injection attempts, 24 of them in a header named X-AI . Most were pranks. The few that ask for real actions only work when the agent holds the matching power, such as a shell or database access. - 139 sites sent a header recording whether they had classified the client as an AI bot, and 136 of them said it was one. Servers already tell agents and people apart, which is the step that agent-only content needs. Audit important sites with an agent’s user agent. - Some sites use headers to push back on agents. Two put strings named after Anthropic’s test triggers in protest-named headers such as X-AI-Makes-Us-Dumber , and one warns hacking agents away on its error pages. Expect your agents to meet text written to stop them as well as to steer them. - 283 distinct header names were aimed at AI, and 1,709 more sites matched our AI keywords without being AI-directed. A detector that matches on names alone would have flagged 910 of those sites by mistake. Alert on what the agent does after a fetch. - In our October 2026 tests, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Haiku running in Claude Code found our test headers and did not act on them by default, and everyday tasks such as an uptime check were enough to put the headers in front of them. When the user’s prompt told them to follow the site’s directions, they obeyed in 7 of 9 runs, so the refusal depends on how much authority your prompts give a site. ## A route most research misses Most research into prompt injection on the web looks at the page itself. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 studied injections on live pages and listed ten ways to deliver them, from zero-size text to URL fragments. None of the ten uses response headers. In its data, social engineering made up 85.2% of jailbreak methods, and the header injections we found fit that: plain “ignore all previous instructions” text with no concealment, because browsers never show headers anyway. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group searched Common Crawl page text and sorted what it found into harmless pranks, helpful guidance, search optimization, deterring AI agents, and malicious. Our header injections lean the same way: 22 of the 30 sites sent pranks, and a few sites used headers to deter agents. So how at risk are agents today? Models are getting better at spotting injected text, but they still follow some of it. In Anthropic’s 2025 tests of Claude for Chrome , attacks succeeded 23.6% of the time without its mitigations and 11.2% with them, so even a hardened agent acted on roughly one attempt in nine. The real risk for any agent comes down to two questions: can hostile text reach its model, and what can the agent do when some of it gets through? This post asks those questions of a route most defenses ignore: the HTTP response headers a server sends with every page. A person reading the page never sees them, but an agent’s tools can pass them straight to the model. We end with what our scan says about the risk today. To see why it matters, start with how indirect prompt injection works. ## Indirect prompt injection Indirect prompt injection is an attack in which instructions reach an AI agent inside content it reads for someone else: a web page, an email, a file, or a tool result. It works because a language model reads its instructions and its data as one stream of text. When you ask an agent to summarize a page, your request and the page land in the same context window, and nothing in the text marks which part may give orders. The user never wrote the injected instructions and usually never sees them. The term comes from a 2023 paper by Greshake and colleagues , and OWASP ranks prompt injection first in its Top 10 for LLM applications. The sequence below shows one attempt from request to result. - 1 Request The user asks for a task "Summarize this page" - 2 Fetch The agent reads content a third party controls page · email · file - 3 Context That content and its hidden text join the prompt data + instructions - 4 Action The model follows the hidden text answer · tool call What step 4 can do depends on the agent’s permissions. A summarizer can only give a skewed answer. An agent that can send email, edit files, or run commands can act on the injected text. ## What a response header is When a browser or an agent requests a URL, the server sends back three parts: a status line that says whether the request worked, a block of header fields that describe the response, and the body, which is the HTML, JSON, or file you asked for. RFC 9110 defines this shape. Headers carry metadata such as the content type, caching rules, and cookies, and a browser shows almost none of them to the reader. The figure below is a short, benign response. The body is the only part a person sees in the browser window. An HTTP response in three parts. Part 1, the status line, reads HTTP/1.1 200 OK and says whether the request worked; it is hidden from the reader. Part 2, the headers, are name and value pairs that describe the response: Content-Type says the body is HTML, Cache-Control sets how long it can be reused, Set-Cookie stores a value in the browser, and X-Request-Id is a custom header the server invented. They are hidden from the reader. Part 3, the body, is the HTML page a person sees in the browser. An agent's fetch tool can pass parts 1 and 2 to the model as text. - 1 Status line Hidden from the reader One line that says whether the request worked. 200 means success. The words after the number are free text the server chooses. HTTP/1.1 200 OK One line that says whether the request worked. 200 means success. The words after the number are free text the server chooses. - 2 Headers Hidden from the reader Name and value pairs that describe the response. Some are standard, and a server can invent any others it likes. Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 The body is an HTML page. Cache-Control: max-age=600 The response can be reused for 10 minutes. Set-Cookie: session=9f2a; HttpOnly Store this value and send it back next time. X-Request-Id: 7d62-4c11 A custom header the server made up. Custom headers like this are where AI-directed text appears. Name and value pairs that describe the response. Some are standard, and a server can invent any others it likes. - 3 Body Shown in the browser The page itself. This is the only part a person reading the site sees.

... The page itself. This is the only part a person reading the site sees. You can see the hidden part of any response yourself. This command sends a normal GET request, prints the headers of every response, follows redirects with -L , and discards the body. Swap in any URL you want to inspect: curl -sS -L -D - -o /dev/null https://signalscorps.com Against our own site it returns two responses, trimmed here to the main fields. The first redirects the bare domain to www , and the second is the page itself: HTTP / 2 301 location : https://www.signalscorps.com/ server : cloudflare HTTP/2 200 content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate link: ; rel="preconnect" server: cloudflare All of that is text a fetch tool could pass to a model. A server can invent any header name it likes, and even the reason phrase on an HTTP/1.1 status line is free text, which RFC 9112 tells clients to ignore. ## How headers reach the model A header only matters to an agent if the agent’s fetch tool copies it into the model’s context. Many tools do not. The ones that do fall into four routes, shown below with a fifth route that drops headers before they arrive. Five routes a response can take from the server to the model. Route one, a shell tool running curl with the dash-i flag, passes every response header. Route two, an error path such as the Gemini CLI direct-fetch mode on a status of 400 or above, passes all headers as JSON without the untrusted wrapper. Route three, a summarizing fetch tool such as Claude Code WebFetch, passes a model-written extract of the page and the redirect target. Route four, the MCP reference fetch server, passes the Content-Type value when a page is not HTML, and the robots.txt body in an error message. Route five, a body-only tool, drops every header before the model sees anything. - Shell tool Runs curl itself curl -i Passes every response header to the model. - Error path Unwrapped on failure status ≥ 400 All headers as JSON, no untrusted wrapper (Gemini CLI direct fetch). - Summarizer Echoes metadata Location Redirect target reaches the model (Claude Code WebFetch). - MCP fetch Echoes edge cases Content-Type Content-Type value on non-HTML pages; robots.txt body in errors. - Body-only tool Drops headers res.text() Only the page content reaches the model. No header gets through. So the question for your own setup is which tool your agent fetches pages with. The short rule: a tool that returns only page text closes this channel, and a shell can open all of it. ## AI headers are already common Headers aimed at AI are already common, and almost all of them are pointers. Of the 7,959 sites in our scan that sent a header addressed to AI, 7,271 used it to point agents to another resource: an llms.txt file, an agents.md file, an MCP server, or an agent skill. One header, x-llms-txt , accounts for 6,989 of those sites. Even a benign pointer is a steering channel. It is a server telling your agent where to go next, including to MCP servers the agent might connect to. Most pointers today lead to documentation. The same header could lead to a file full of instructions or a tool server the site owner controls. This chart counts each site once, under the most serious label any of its headers received. Pointer to an agent resource: 7,271 sites. AI policy or description: 511 sites. AI-client detection: 139 sites. Injection attempt: 30 sites. Guidance to AI: 8 sites. - Pointer llms.txt, MCP servers, agent skills 7,271 - Policy or description Crawl, training, and content claims 511 - AI-client detection Server reports its AI-bot check 139 - Injection attempt Tries to override the agent 30 - Guidance How to use the content 8 The eight guidance sites sit between pointers and injections. Half tell an agent how to use the site without overriding it, for example by asking it to prefer a JSON API over scraping the HTML.
